records.text: , cooling electricity consumption has already increased by ~50% since 2015 to ~2.9trn units, and we estimate incremental cooling demand (excluding data centers) could be as large as incremental electricity demand from data centers. Asia is particularly exposed as rising AC ownership compounds higher utilisation rates. The implication is that cooling adds not only energy demand, but also disproportionately increases the need for peak generation, storage and grid capacity. Asia: We forecast Asia's installed AC stock will increase from ~1.1bn units today to ~1.4bn by 2030. We also assume running hours rise ~3.4% a year as temperatures increase. On that basis, we estimate cooling electricity demand rises from ~1.5trn units in 2025 to ~2.1trn units by 2030 (~7% CAGR). This would increase cooling's share of total Asian electricity demand from ~10% to ~11%, and account for ~15% of the total growth in electricity consumption that we forecast through 2030. Europe: MS forecasts heat-pump penetration will increase from 15% of households today to 19% by 2030 (Exhibit 72). Assuming average annual electricity consumption of 4,000kWh per unit (within a range of 3,000–5,000kWh), we estimate heat-pump electricity demand rises from 113TWh in 2025 to 179TWh by 2030. This would increase heat pumps' share of total European electricity demand from 3.8% to 5.4% (Exhibit 21), and account for 21% of the total growth in electricity consumption that we forecast through 2030.

Hiring tends to lag growth as employers await several months of sustained demand before adding permanent staff. Continued consumer demand should therefore bolster employment in the coming months, all else equal. We expect the BoC to prioritise inflation and deliver a 25bps hike at the 26 Oct meeting, consistent with our hawkish dovish index reaching its highest level since Oct 2023. Terms of trade remain a major economic tailwind (Figure 3). Canada supplied 63% of US crude imports in 2025, making it crucial to US oil security as the US draws down its SPR reserves. The Trans Mountain pipeline has further diversified exports and expanded access to Pacific and Asian markets, strengthening Canada’s leverage. These factors should support growth in the coming months and reinforce the case for the BoC to deliver the hikes currently priced in. Together with renewed buying by real money, this supports our constructive medium term CAD outlook. Cooling therefore rises from ~10% to ~11% of Asia’s electricity consumption, adding almost ~0.6tn units of annual demand by the end of the decade, while Europe will also need similar amount of power for heat pumps making up 5%+ of total power consumption share. China remains the largest cooling market in absolute terms, but growth is increasingly coming from lower-penetration economies. We estimate India’s cooling demand will nearly double to ~280bn units by 2030, while Vietnam, Malaysia and the Philippines should also grow at high-single to low-double-digit rates. The pressure on the power system is greater than the annual TWh figures suggest: The IEA estimates cooling accounts for only around 10% of global electricity consumption but ~30% of peak power demand, with ~1,400GW of cooling-related peak load in 2025. In India, cooling demand accounted for 40% of peak power demand in 2026 due to El Niño conditions. records.text: M Idea Morgan Stanley Research 3 Clearing Events Still Ahead The equity markets have been correcting since June. We identified this correction as a mid- cycle transition that coincided with the initial peak rate of change in earnings revision breadth that arrived after a recessionary low—in this case, the Rolling Recession trough which was reached near Liberation Day. Early cycle stocks (semis, financials, consumer cyclicals) tend to underperform during this transition as the market moves toward higher quality factors. Mid-cycle transition winners include more asset-light, services-oriented stocks with lower operating and financial leverage—i.e., quality. Over the past month, we have been wrestling with the wide divergence between the poor breadth of the market and the resilience of the S&P 500 Index (Exhibit 1 ). This too is typical during mid-cycle transitions when the market rotates toward quality. After all, there is no higher quality large cap index in the world than the S&P 500, so it makes sense for investors to crowd into the S&P 500 during this transition. Exhibit 1: The S&P 500 and breadth measures are starting to converge by meeting in the middle, as we suggested a few weeks ago. This is a sign we are getting closer to the end of the correction. Source: Bloomberg, Morgan Stanley Research In addition to a peaking rate of change in earnings revisions, we also typically witness a Fed pivoting toward a more hawkish stance as growth runs too hot and inflation shows up.

records.text: M Global Insight 52 China China benefits from the 'powering everything' cycle, but it is not a US-style power shortage trade. We expect overall electricity demand to grow at around 5% CAGR towards 2035, primarily driven by electrification. The investment question is less whether China can produce enough electricity nationally than how it delivers dependable power at the right time and price. We prefer defensive power generators with low cost, flexible generation capability and resilient cash flows. Yangtze Power is our most preferred stock in this thesis. Demand - modest industrial growth; data centres and EV charging are bright spots. We forecast industrial electricity demand to grow at a 3.7% CAGR over 2025-30, below overall power demand growth. However, we see stronger growth coming from EV charging and data centres. We expect data centre power demand at ~664TWh by 2030, or about 5% of national consumption, compared to 2% in 2025. EV charging is another structural driver as EV penetrates - electricity use by charging services grew 55.4% YoY to 131.5bn kWh in 9M26. This represents 1.6% of the overall power demand, compared to 0.1% five years ago. Supply - structural transition continues; flexibility and interconnection to be key. Wind and solar, alongside hydropower and nuclear, should continue taking share from fossil generation, in our view. records.text: Metal Matters 26 October 2026 Citi Research 2 October is seasonally the strongest month for India gold and silver imports. Based on import data over 2011-26, October silver imports averaged 1.73x of LT monthly average imports, while October gold imports averaged 1.23x of LT monthly average imports. On average, India imported ~25Moz of silver and ~2.5Moz of gold in October. This seasonal strength is driven by festive demand during Navratri and Dussehra, with Diwali occasionally falling in October, as well as improved rural liquidity following the Kharif harvest in September and October. Import volumes for both metals are typically moderate after October. However, November remains the second-strongest month for gold imports, averaging 1.19x of LT monthly average imports, supported by years when Diwali falls in November and by stronger wedding-related demand, which may benefit from school holidays during the Diwali period. In their mind, because monetary policy works by steering demand, and because transmission lags can be long, it can only affect inflation at a relatively long horizon. In the three-pillar framework used by the ECB currently, they would place relatively more emphasis on the last two. “Hawks” , by contrast, are central bankers who put much more emphasis on inflation expectations in the formation of prices. If one believes that inflation expectations impact on future prices, and if one recognises (reasonably) that current inflation has a bearing on inflation expectations, then one will be much less patient in the face of a shock. Hawks are more backward-looking, more willing to consider that any deviation of realised inflation requires a policy response, because of the risk of de-anchoring of expectations that they assume. In the three-pillar framework of the ECB, they would pay more attention to the first. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: A Moderate Boost to DM Inflation from AI Demand Global central bankers are increasingly citing the AI buildout as an inflation driver. Comments have generally focused on the risks from supply bottlenecks and higher import prices, as well as the potential timing mismatch between near-term domestic demand pressures and more lagged and uncertain productivity gains (Exhibit 1). In this Global Economics Comment, we refresh our global model (extending our US team’s recent analysis of US inflation pressures stemming from AI) to estimate the inflation impulses from AI investment in DM economies. We continue to consider three main channels through which the AI capex cycle is directly boosting inflation: the direct boost to consumer prices from higher memory prices, spillovers from higher memory prices to consumer electronics, and the increase in electricity prices associated with increased data center power demand.1 First, increased demand for memory from data centers has led to outsized increases in memory prices. This is directly boosting consumer prices for memory cards, but in most countries the effect of these increases remains minimal (2-3bp on year-over-year core inflation) due to the tiny weight of memory cards in overall inflation baskets. records.text: M Global Insight 40 United States While more data center capacity is shifting abroad, we do not believe there is sufficient capacity in the rest of the world to absorb the entire US net power shortfall (43GW from 2026–28) (Exhibit 44 ). Companies are increasingly looking overseas for capacity, with Nvidia recently noting that Australia is a region “with excess energy” where it has lined up 2GW for 2027. Reflecting these developments, we include expectations of US Data Center spillover into APAC. Though we expect international expansion to continue, we do not view it as a panacea for the US power challenge. Conversations with our European data center analyst, Emmet Kelly, suggest there is limited scope for additional spillover into Europe given power constraints and slow planning approvals (see more here). While expansion into the Middle East remains a possibility, we believe geopolitical instability presents a meaningful challenge (see example of AWS data center affected by Iran strikes). Our Asia data center team already assumes 15GW of US hyperscaler demand shifts to Asia through 2030 (Exhibit 30), yet we still forecast a US power shortfall despite that demand migration. Any additional spillover would likely require greater reliance on energy sources such as coal. While companies are willing to build data centers abroad, we do not believe sufficient capacity exists to absorb the US power shortfall. We do see potential upside to our forecast from behind-the-meter generation.

We see a few reasons. First, PuFins spending is ‘costless’ from a fiscal rules perspective. Indeed, investment via financial transactions won’t impact either of the Chancellor’s fiscal rules. On the Chancellor’s debt rule, financial transactions will be net -neutral, with equity injections or loans generating both an asset and a liability on the government’s balance sheet. Higher interest or equity valuation could even reduce public sector net financial liabilities – the government’s preferred debt measure. records.text: M Global Insight Morgan Stanley Research 71 Australia • We estimate Australian grid electricity demand growth at ~1% per annum to 2030, compared with a decline of 0.6% per annum in the decade prior to GenAI. • We estimate data centers could account for 6–14% (17-38TWh) of underlying electricity demand by 2030, up from ~3% (~7TWh) today. • Australia's duck curve is flattening as battery deployment accelerates, making the National Electricity Market a global case study. • With equipment cost inflation, we remain constructive on medium-term power- price growth, which should support the integrated utilities in our coverage: AGL Energy and Origin Energy. Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg Source: Citi Research, Bloomberg Imports in value terms highlight a notable divergence in the price sensitivity of gold and silver demand. Gold demand has historically exhibited a stronger relationship with GDP growth, while silver demand appears less tied to economic growth and more resilient to higher prices. Despite a sharp rise in precious metals prices in 2026, Indian spending on both metals in US dollar terms remained broadly stable compared to 2025, with lower import volumes offset by higher prices. Between 2011-19 and 2020-26, silver prices increased by approximately 57%, yet the value of silver imports rose by 51% while import volumes declined by only 7%, indicating relatively price-inelastic demand. In contrast, gold prices increased by 86% over the same period, but the value of gold imports rose by 27% as import volumes declined by 27%. This suggests gold demand is more sensitive to higher prices than silver demand. We believe this reflects silver's dual role as both an investment and industrial metal, while gold demand in India remains predominantly driven by jewelry and physical investment. Additionally, elevated gold prices may be encouraging some degree of substitution towards silver. Prepared for Cayla Buettner

records.text: This Agriculture Analyst offers a brief primer on the coffee market and our n outlook. The physical market should loosen as a strong 2026/27 crop is expected to push the global market into surplus. Because only a small share of global coffee is eligible for delivery against ICE futures, low ICE certified stocks could keep the futures curve in backwardation and front-month prices highly volatile even as physical supply improves this year, while early signs point to renewed supply risks in 2027/28. Good: The physical market should loosen in 2026/27. Coffee prices have n already fallen in anticipation of a strong crop, with Arabica (the premium bean) down ~10% YTD and robusta (the cheaper bean used in instant coffee) down ~15% YTD. Brazil (~45% of global arabica production) has harvested a strong arabica crop (47.5mn bags, up ~25% YoY), while the robusta harvest in Vietnam (~40% of global robusta production) is also expected to be strong (31.4mn bags, up ~3% YoY) after ample irrigation water earlier this year (which we nowcast through NASA satellite imagery). The USDA expects global coffee production to exceed consumption by ~10 million bags (~6%) in 2026/27. Bad: The 2027/28 crop is already at risk. Brazil’s arabica trees typically produce n less after a large crop, making 2027 an off-year following the strong 2026 harvest. This means that the FOMC is set to skip raising rates at its October meeting but is likely to deliver a second hike in December. The Fed’s hawkish pivot has contributed to a large increase in interest rates that n has driven a moderate tightening since September in broad financial conditions, which before then had been little changed on net this year. But the tightening is only a bit more than is usually associated with one rate hike and much less than is usually associated with the four hikes the market has now priced, meaning that the FOMC is unlikely to see it as excessive or a replacement for hikes. A key question for the October meeting this week is how the FOMC will modify n the sentence in its statement that refers to the hike at the September meeting. We think it might adapt language from Vice Chair Jefferson’s recent speech to say, “ Any further adjustments to the target range for the federal funds rate to support a timelier return to the Committee’s 2 percent goal will depend on trends in the data, the evolving outlook, and the balance of risks.” We do not expect significant new information from the press conference. records.text: 5. Our own base case remains that AI investment will ultimately pay off in terms of higher productivity and economywide profits. However, one key channel for this payoff is labor market disruption, which has negative near-term macroeconomic effects. And while DM labor markets still look solid in aggregate, we are starting to see clearer signs that the AI impact is spreading beyond the technology sector. Across nonmanufacturing industries, the share of US firms that have adopted AI in regular business functions now shows a statistically significant negative correlation with employment growth and a statistically significant positive correlation with unemployment. 6. The Fed’s recent signals—explicit from Williams/Je fferson and implicit from Warsh— effectively rule out a hike on October 28. This takes us again to the discussion of what constitutes a “dove” or a “hawk” . Those labels are often used but rarely explained. In a recent interview (La Croix, 30 September), Christine Lagarde described hawks as individuals “who favour tightening monetary policy to fight inflation” , while doves would be those “who are keen to support economic activity with accommodative monetary policy” . Those definitions seem to imply that the doves are more willing than the hawks to compromise on the central bank’s primary objective. Our own definition is entirely different. It recognises that both hawks and doves are equally committed to the central bank mandate, but that they have different understanding of how prices are formed, and that this translates into noticeably different reaction functions. “Doves” , in our interpretation, are central bankers who believe that inflation is primarily a matter of the confrontation of supply and demand. Economists of this obedience will be very sensitive to the origin of a shock to prices. They will be very keen to respond if the shock is endogenous (a shock to demand, or a persistent shock to supply), but will show substantial patience if the shock is exogenous (such as is the case now). In our reading of past policy decisions, this pillar also includes a backward-looking element, because we believe that realised inflation does affect the interpretation of this first pillar, and we explain below how we rationalise this observation. The second dimension of the framework is the underlying dynamics of inflation. We see this as encompassing all the information that allows to distinguish between endogenous and exogenous price shocks. In the current circumstances, for instance, it relates to the emergence, or lack thereof, of second round effects. That means in particular the question of whether higher energy prices will feed into higher wages. This should be the critical point of interest, as second round effects must include wages. We do not believe there can take place a price-price loop (where higher prices feed into higher prices) without there being a wage-price loop (where higher prices feed into higher wages). records.text: 26 October 2026 Focus Germany Deutsche Bank AG Page 7 Meanwhile, the budget deficits at the state and municipal levels look poised to remain close to last year's levels. The municipal deficit in particular will likely stay highly elevated, weighed down by a high structural base for personnel and social spending alongside sluggish revenue growth (2025 deficit: EUR 31 bn or about 0.7% of GDP). This trend is underscored by H1 2026 developments, where the deficit matched the high levels seen in H1 2025 (see Figure 15). All in all, at a forecast 4.2% of GDP , we expect the general government deficit to widen noticeably this year, albeit remaining lower than the government's projection of 4.75% (see Germany Draft Budgetary Plan 2027). This is, among other things, because defense and federal investment spending might once again fall short of their ambitious targets this year, and partly because Germany's economic growth momentum should prove more resilient than assumed in the official deficit projection (implying a smaller negative output gap and thus a lower cyclical deficit). While the general government deficit appears set to expand further in 2027, our forecast of 4.7% of GDP continues to be below the government's projected 5.25% (see Figure 16 and Figure 17). records.text: Economics 26 October 2026 Citi Research 5 At this stage, we underline that neither constituency is “hawkish” or “dovish” in the traditional sense. Both are equally committed to price stability, but their horizon is different because of how much they believe the expectations channel matters in relation to other channels. Where this difference translates into the commonly accepted understanding of “hawks” and “doves” is via the aversion for error that each constituency will rationally exhibit. That is important, because as we have argued from time to time, human behaviour is not motivated solely by what we want to achieve, but also by what we most want to avoid. This is true of all of us, irrespective of our walk of life. It is certainly true of central bankers. They cannot avoid policy mistakes, and so will naturally have a bias – this is to be put to their credit – to prefer a policy mistake whose consequences they can control to one whose consequences they cannot. Since doves generally believe inflation to be a matter of supply and demand, they know they can always bring inflation down from levels above target. This can be achieved by destruction of demand, which monetary policy can always deliver. If inflation were to fall towards zero, however, the experience of the 2010s in Europe and the US, that of the US in the 1930s and that of Japan over much of the past three decades is less encouraging. We do not deviate from tradition, but we do it this month in an unusual way. Rather than focusing on immediate decisions, we discuss below whether the reaction function of the European Central Bank (ECB) may change - and why - when the President leaves her position. The reason we do this now is threefold: first, we believe that the past few months illustrate that the ECB reaction function has not been stable. Second, it seems to us rational to expect that the President of the ECB might announce very soon her early departure from the ECB, which will immediately raise questions as to what that implies for the direction of policy. Third, it gives us again an opportunity to explain what a “hawk” or a “dove” really means in the context of monetary policy. 1. Three pillars, but not equally weighed We start this short discussion with the “framework” that the leadership of the ECB regularly quotes as the guide to their decisions. records.text: 26 October 2026 Focus Germany Page 2 Deutsche Bank AG A look at the MoF's October 2026 Monthly Report In this update, we take a look at the October 2026 Monthly Report from the Federal Ministry of Finance (MoF), which contains the financial statistics data on federal budget developments for the first nine months of the year. The analysis builds on our previous work regarding Germany's fiscal policy shift (see also here and here). It considers the latest dynamics of a) the federal government's core budget as well as b) the two major off-budgetary funds SV BW (Federal Armed Forces Fund) and SV IK (Infrastructure & Climate Neutrality Fund) for which the government provides monthly credit stock/flow data.1 The MoF's September 2026 budget print Monthly budgetary developments in a nutshell As Figure 1 illustrates, the total federal financing deficit (comprising the core budget, SV BW, and SV IK) moderated by roughly EUR 6 bn to about EUR 160 bn in September on a 12-month smoothed basis (approx. 3.4% of 2026F GDP; full-year target: EUR 182 bn or 3.9%). Consequently, the total deficit, based on the trailing 12-month sum, has expanded by nearly EUR 100 bn since the 2025 federal budget took effect in October last year. Early signs are already emerging, with industrial power demand beginning to trend higher (Exhibit 41). We estimate steel, autos, semiconductors, defence, refining, chemicals and related industries could add around 2trn units of incremental power consumption by 2030, implying CAGR of 3.43% over 2025–30, roughly 1.5x faster than the previous decade. Industrialisation remains the largest contributor to power-consumption growth in Asia: We forecast industrial electricity consumption in Asia will grow at a ~4% CAGR, accounting for 43% of the region's incremental electricity demand and growing at roughly 2.7x the rate of data center consumption (Exhibit 48). We have already seen improving industrial electricity-demand trends across Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Japan during 2025 and 1H26 (Exhibit 41). Semiconductors, automobiles, chemicals, metals and mining, as well as food processing, are among the sectors that have recorded higher electricity consumption over the past 18 months. records.text: China’s property downturn is now in its sixth year. While we had projected the n property sector’s drag to real GDP growth to narrow somewhat from last year to this year, most housing activity indicators have been much weaker than anticipated so far this year. In addition, the recently announced shift from presales to completed-home sales implies tighter developer funding and lower property investment over the next few years. In this note, we update our estimates of the property sector’s contribution to real GDP growth to reflect the year-to-date data and this policy change. Our updated estimates suggest that the property market’s share of China’s real n GDP will decline from around 15% currently (vs. nearly 30% at its peak) to around 8% from 2030 onward. Adding up five direct channels – construction, real estate services, upstream effects (through commodity demand), move-in related consumption and land sales related fiscal channels – we estimate a 1.8pp drag on real GDP growth in 2026, slightly larger than 1.7pp in 2025. We expect this direct drag to narrow by around 0.5pp to 1.3pp in 2027 and largely fade by 2030. Including the indirect housing wealth effect amplifies the estimated growth impact, but this does not change our conclusion that the property sector’s drag on real GDP growth should gradually diminish over the coming years. It shows that the zero lower bound is binding, and that reflationary policies then become difficult, and possibly unavailable to the central bank without assistance from governments. So central bankers of this constituency may be marginally less adverse to inflation being a bit too high than a bit too low. The weight put by hawks on expectations leads to a diametrically opposed conclusion. If expectations matter, then the consequences of inflation undershooting are less worrying than those of inflation overshooting. Downward nominal rigidity means that deviation of inflation from target on the downside can be persistent but are unlikely to be very large. Indeed, during the 2010s, inflation hovered fairly close to zero in Europe but outright deflation never materialised. There is no similar stickiness of prices on the upside and so, if as in 2022 there occurs a very large exogenous shock in that direction, inflation can quickly rise far above target. If the size of deviation of inflation from target is relevant to expectations, and if expectations drive prices, then the conclusion has to be that it is less dangerous for the central bank to undershoot the target than to overshoot it. records.text: ncluding behind-the-meter generation, fuel cells and nuclear, we estimate the US could still face power shortfalls of ~43GW by 2028 and 80GW by 2029 (Exhibit 46). Our bottom-up Asia work suggests the region could absorb ~15GW of this shortfall, supported by available data center capacity and power supply, with Thailand, Malaysia, India and Japan among the markets seeing rising hyperscaler commitments (Exhibit 30). This represents power demand that can move faster than new US grid infrastructure can be built, increasing the value of available capacity and time-to-power in Asia. We expect dependable generation – particularly natural gas alongside renewables and storage – to play an important role in supporting this incremental load. More efficient compute is not reducing absolute power requirements. New rack-scale architectures produce substantially more tokens and compute per watt, but system designers are using these efficiency gains to deploy more computing capacity. Larger models and more complex workloads also require greater memory, networking, cooling and sustained utilization – particularly for reasoning and agentic workloads. As a result, absolute rack power continues to rise even as the cost of intelligence falls. (Exhibit 31)

records.text: an Stanley Research In addition to a peaking rate of change in earnings revisions, we also typically witness a Fed pivoting toward a more hawkish stance as growth runs too hot and inflation shows up. While others have focused on the war in Iran and the spike in energy prices as the primary reasons for inflation and higher back-end rates, we have argued it's been mostly about stronger-than-expected nominal GDP growth dragging both the front-end pricing and back-end rates higher (Exhibit 2 ). Warsh's desire to let markets trade to fair value also inspired traders to embrace this theme. This was core to our "run it hot" thesis from the summer of 2025, which inevitably reached a point where the Fed had to react. We reached that point in June, and the Fed has chosen to let the market do most of the work via back-end rates and fed funds re-pricing. Meanwhile, they have slowed the rate of balance sheet expansion by about half (Exhibit 3 ), which helps to explain why the rotations have been more violent than normal, in our view. This was further amplified by the significant crowding in the price momentum factor levered to early cycle stocks (i.e., semis).

In our reading, whether any individual central banker is closer to the definition of a hawk or a dove cannot be identified solely from their inclination to hike or cut rates at a given moment in time. It is better assessed by looking at the frequency of references to the output gap or to inflation expectations in their communication and in their description of the economy. The reason why we gave this (stylised) explanation of what it really means to be a dove or a hawk is that when a new President takes up the position at the ECB, we expect the central bank reaction function to be relatively more stable than it has been recently, if the new President has a more clearly articulated view on what matters most to price formation. records.text: Arabica and robusta meet in the blend When arabica becomes more expensive than usual relative to robusta, roasters can use more robusta, but only until taste becomes a constraint. The two prices therefore move together, but imperfectly. The futures market: the warehouse matters as much as the harvest Arabica futures trade on ICE New York in US cents/lb and robusta on ICE London in $/tonne, but physical coffee rarely trades at the screen price. Exporters sell at a premium or discount depending on origin and quality. In that sense, coffee is a bit like wine: region, variety and quality all matter. While the harvest determines how much coffee is available globally, certified stocks help determine front-month futures volatility. Certified stocks are the smaller pool of coffee that meets exchange standards and can be delivered against futures. When that pool is scarce, nearby futures can spike even if coffee remains available elsewhere (Exhibit 7, Right Panel). Certified stocks generally move with global inventories and have fallen alongside them following several years of deficits since 2021 (Exhibit 7). But they can also be constrained by exchange rules, quality requirements and the economics of delivering coffee onto the exchange. A good harvest therefore only eases futures-market tightness if enough of those beans can replenish certified stocks. Replenishment has recently become more difficult. records.text: M Global Insight Morgan Stanley Research 47 Asia: Energy Security & Powering AI “Digital infrastructure and energy infrastructure can no longer be planned separately.”, COO PETRONAS, Malaysia “SoftBank… launched a Japan-based battery business aimed at building next- generation power infrastructure to support the rapidly increasing demand for electricity being driven by AI adoption.” Securing energy supply for AI has emerged as a durable, system‑level investment theme across the power and fuel value chains, distinct from decarbonization targets or short‑term price signals. Recent LNG disruptions and extreme price volatility have shifted policy-maker and corporate behavior toward reliability, dispatchability, and domestic or regional resilience over pure economic optimization. We think this will drive a new sustained capex cycle across grid infrastructure, battery storage, strategic reserves, utilities, and selective generation technologies. Second (and the biggest change relative to our last update), higher memory prices are starting to spill into consumer prices for electronic goods such as phones, computers and video game consoles, which have much higher weights in global inflation baskets. These consumer electronics categories are currently contributing less than 0.1pp to year-over-year core inflation across DMs (Exhibit 2, right), with the largest boosts in Japan and US PCE. In this Global Economics Comment, we refresh our global model (extending our US team’s recent analysis of US inflation pressures stemming from AI) to assess the size of AI-related inflation risks. Direct inflation pressures from the AI buildout are currently limited in most n economies (around 0.1pp) because categories directly exposed to memory prices receive smaller weights outside of US core PCE (where memory is adding 19bp). records.text: October FOMC Preview: Hiking at a Slower Pace Comments from FOMC participants since their last meeting point to a compromise to raise the funds rate every other meeting. As our latest FOMC Chatterbox highlighted, participants have said that they do not see “urgency” to deliver additional hikes and that hikes “do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” as Governor Waller put it. An every-other-meeting pace means that the FOMC, having just hiked in September, is set to skip raising rates at its October meeting this week but is likely to deliver a second hike in December. This is in line with our forecast, which calls for a second and final hike in December. The Fed’s hawkish pivot has contributed to a large increase in interest rates that has driven a moderate tightening since September in our Financial Conditions Index, which until then had been little changed this year because higher rates had been offset by higher stock prices and narrower credit spreads (Exhibit 1, left). The 30bp tightening in our FCI is only a bit more than is usually associated with one 25bp rate hike and is much less than is usually associated with the four hikes the market has now priced or the even larger turnaround in expectations for where the funds rate will stand by 2027 since the start of the year (Exhibit 1, right). M Global Insight 32 AI Needs Power; Grid Needs Time and Batteries The power curve is changing shape across most markets, creating higher margins for generators that can supply flexible capacity and for batteries that can discharge quickly (Exhibit 37). However, it also reduces returns for renewables. Data centers, together with batteries, energy storage systems and EVs, should make daily power demand more stable, albeit at higher levels. This will come at a cost to consumers, as power grids will need to become significantly more flexible. One common trend is the growing spread between daily peak and trough demand. The steepness of the demand curve continues to increase across markets, driven not only by renewable penetration but also by rising industrial power consumption. The changing shape of the power curve is adding to inflationary pressure in electricity prices as grid investment requirements increase. We estimate Asia will require around US$1trn of power-grid investment through 2030 (Exhibit 39) to accommodate rising electricity demand and greater system flexibility. We believe data centers will partially fund these investments by absorbing higher power tariffs, while also increasing the attractiveness of behind-the-meter power supply arrangements for generation companies. records.text: Economics 26 October 2026 Citi Research 4 expect that the next President may have more clearly articulated views on the reaction function of the central bank. Our first assertion is substantiated by the already mentioned fact that in the next few months, the three most important positions on the six-member Executive Board of the ECB will change hands (and even possibly four positions). Our current expectation is that the new President will be one of the two candidates most often cited in the media, i.e. Pablo Hernandez de Cos and Klaas Knot (Bloomberg 23October). Both have considerable expertise, experience and reputation. Both have been closely involved in monetary policy and other ECB policies for decades. Both know the ECB itself and the Eurosystem closely. By contrast the German and French Executive Board members, who will replace Isabel Schnabel (in January) and Philip Lane (in June) are likely to be relative newcomers. The same observation applies to some extent to the Governing Council. Few Governors (with the possible exception of Fabio Panetta) appear to combine the depth and breadth of experience that both Pablo Hernandez de Cos and Klaas Knot have accumulated over the years. records.text: M Global Insight 54 Europe Following a recent inflection point, we expect power-demand growth in Europe to accelerate over the coming years, driven by the rise of data centers and a broader acceleration in electrification across European economies. We forecast European power demand will grow at a 2.2% CAGR over 2026–30 and 2.3% over 2026–35, with some European markets matching or even exceeding power-demand growth rates in the US. We believe rising power demand will benefit the utilities sector through higher power prices, stronger pricing power for flexible assets (CCGTs and batteries), improved returns on investment in generation, flexibility and grid infrastructure, and the increasing strategic value of powered land that can potentially be monetised. Unlike some developed markets, where electricity demand has historically been relatively flat and data centers are emerging as a major source of incremental consumption, LatAm's power demand outlook remains largely driven by economic growth, industrial activity, population growth, electrification and the rising penetration of electrical appliances. These structural factors should continue to support electricity consumption across the region, although growth rates will vary by country depending on economic conditions, industrial development and energy policies. As a result, we expect power demand to continue expanding even without a meaningful contribution from data centers. Data centers could accelerate demand growth, despite not being the main driver. The rapid expansion of AI, cloud computing and digital infrastructure is creating a new source of electricity demand globally, with LatAm increasingly attracting interest from developers given its renewable resources, relatively competitive energy costs and proximity to major markets. However, unlike in the US, where large-scale data center investments are becoming a key driver of incremental load, we expect the contribution in LatAm to remain relatively modest compared with traditional demand drivers, at least through the end of the decade. records.text: rtified stocks could keep the futures curve in backwardation and front-month prices highly volatile even as physical supply improves this year. ICE arabica stocks fell to 218k bags in September, their lowest since 1999, and remain around 228k today. That leaves the front-month contract vulnerable to sharp squeezes, even with ample global supply this year. Rebuilding stocks may also be slow: physical coffee currently commands better prices than exchange delivery, some of the strong Brazilian arabica crop may not meet ICE quality requirements (due to heavy rainfall during harvest), and the EU deforestation regulation creates additional uncertainty around existing European certified stocks. For instance, about 78% of certified arabica stocks are “transition” coffee at EU ports (mostly Antwerp) that may face a delivery discount from 2027. France’s fiscal troubles and higher long-end yields are doing some of the ECB’s tightening, while energy pass-through into core inflation remains limited. December may stay live, but the bar for tightening beyond that is rising. The ECB’s hawkish summer has given way to a more cautious autumn. Our measure of monetary tone for the ECB has fallen back towards neutral, while markets have pared pack rate expectations from their late-summer highs (Figure 1). December remains live, but keeping the option open is different from signalling a sequence of hikes. With higher borrowing costs already adding restraint, the burden of proof increasingly falls on broader inflation pass-through. So far, the evidence offers little support. This architecture demands significantly higher counts of MLCCs and power modules for more complex power management. The market expects these platforms to drive substantial revenue growth across the AI supply chain into under-construction and planned data centers. Consequently, growing uncertainty over AI investment and agentic AI adoption poses a major risk, potentially compressing valuation multiples for related stocks. We examine five concerns below. Capital bottlenecks stalling AI investment: Demand for compute capacity significantly outstrips supply, creating vast funding requirements to bridge the gap and providing opportunities for banking and private credit. If one does not know whether policy rates are neutral or restrictive, it is not clear to us how policy transmission is assessed. More recently, the balance of weight put on the three pillars seems to have changed. In her hearing at the European Parliament on 28 September, the President emphasised the second and third pillar, underlying the lack of evidence that higher energy prices feed into wages, and the rise in long-term yields, which slow growth and reduce pass-through from an exogenous price shock. This seems to place the ECB now broadly in the position we mistakenly thought it would be in September: a situation where, with policy rates at the upper end of the neutral range, the bar for further tightening becomes higher. Our expectations then were that a minority of “dovish” Council members would be able to reduce the appetite for additional rate hikes, even in the context of a deterioration of near term inflation projections, because they would demand evidence of the emergence of second round effects to take policy into properly restrictive territory. The policy statement and press conference that followed the September meeting contradicted our expectation. Communication since seems to bring it back into the field of probable. We have accordingly not changed our baseline expectation that the Governing Council will leave policy rates unchanged this week, probably hike them by 25 bp

records.text: M Global Idea 2 Rethinking Gold as a Safe Haven Serena Tang, Yimin Huang Parts of the last few weeks have evoked memories of 2022–2023, when correlations between stock and bond returns surged and both markets declined in tandem, leaving investors with supposedly well-diversified portfolios that offered little protection. While we've had interesting debates with investors on why stock-bond correlations are "breaking" once again, one question we've been fielding with increasing frequency has been whether this is gold's time to shine again as the safe haven in portfolios. Our analysis suggests the answer is yes – but with an important caveat: it depends on what investors are trying to keep their portfolios safe from: • Historically, gold has been a less effective diversifier of equity risk, given its volatility is comparable to that of stocks. In fact, prior to 2006, adding gold to a traditional stock-bond portfolio did little to improve its efficient frontier. • But since 2006, gold has helped portfolios, it's just that it's been via strong returns, not risk reduction. It didn’t lower the floor on portfolio risk, and gold only made a difference by pushing out the efficient frontiers in years in which it beat bonds by more than 8.5%. • Pre-2020, gold was a good enough equity hedge: It was a strong safe haven in extreme weekly sell-offs, and also a safe haven from USTs in their worst months. • Since 2020, gold has amplified equity drawdowns rather than cushioning them. The indirect housing wealth effect has amplified the property sector growth impact Our estimates above primarily capture the property sector’s direct impact on real GDP growth, but second-round effects—particularly through housing wealth—also matter. As property represents more than half of Chinese household assets, changes in home values can materially affect confidence and consumption (Exhibit 7). Building on our previous household balance-sheet study, we estimate this indirect channel from 2017 onward (due to data availability constraints). Specifically, we multiply urban property values by the change in our constructed secondary-market property price series to calculate the annual change in household housing wealth. We then apply our estimated wealth-effect coefficient, under which a RMB1 change in property value is associated with a RMB0.01 change in annual household consumption in the same direction, to gauge the GDP impact through this indirect channel. Based on our estimates, the negative housing wealth effect peaked in 2024-25. Assuming nationwide existing home prices bottoming in 2030 as our property research team expects, this negative housing wealth effect should gradually subside in coming years before fully disappearing in early 2030s (Exhibit 8). This is a function of bond returns falling over the last 20 years or so while returns for the precious metal went in the other direction. Exhibit 6 shows efficient frontiers of various combinations of stocks, USTs, and gold, but this time only using performance data since 2006. The results tell a very different story: across all achievable levels of portfolio volatility, including gold would have delivered higher returns than a portfolio without it. Put another way, at any given level of expected return, adding gold would have allowed investors to achieve that return with less risk. Results and week ahead. Valuations LME Week: copper conviction wanes, aluminium outlook bearish LME Week took place last week, bringing together miners, traders, customers and other market participants. The overall tone was relatively bearish, with noticeably less optimism than last year. Macro concerns dominated, with the ongoing unwind of the AI trade, persistent inflation and interest-rate concerns weighing on sentiment. Copper remains the preferred metal, but conviction has weakened. AI-related demand is still seen as a key demand driver, although some participants believe expectations have become overblown. Doubts persist around whether the US will impose a tariff on refined copper, with US imports expected to slow in the months ahead. The concentrate market remains exceptionally tight, with TC/RCs falling to new lows and growing expectations that the annual TC/RC benchmark could fragment towards shorter term and more regional deals. There is a broad expectation that mine supply will recover in 2027, but we expect companies to lower production guidance in the months ahead, while any meaningful supply rebound will be H2’27 weighted. We also suspect that some FOMC participants share our views that the economy is not overheated and that the inflation overshoot caused by past supply shocks will largely have to be waited out because the employment costs of offsetting them by tightening monetary policy to reduce demand would be too great. FOMC participants who share these views might prefer to limit the total size of the Fed’s hiking package. Finally, some participants might have been on the fence about the effectiveness of rate hikes but might have seen gradual and limited hikes as largely harmless from a starting point where growth and the labor market were solid. If concerns about growth or employment emerged—perhaps as a result of higher energy prices eroding real income and weighing on consumer spending, or a more substantial tightening in financial conditions than seen so far—they would likely want to stop raising the funds rate. That is 25.5bp in a little over three months, two-thirds of the 39bp distance to the target. We mark the gain as the change in the new-issue spread times the 20y DV01 at entry. The spread narrowed 25.5bp, worth +3.63 yen per 100 yen face of the 20y. Carry is slightly negative, -0.05 yen (-0.4bp equivalent), because the coupon paid on the 5y short (2.0% on 3.04 times the face) exceeds the 3.7% earned on the 20y even after the repo received (Tokyo repo rate, overnight: 1.00% to 23 September, 1.25% from 24 September). The total is +3.58 yen, or +25.1bp in DV01 terms; on a JPY1bn 20y leg (JPY3.04bn of 5y) that is about JPY36mn. The worst mark was +5.0bp on the day after entry (about -0.7 yen); the position never came close to the 180bp stop and has been in profit every day since 4 September. records.text: ect the contribution in LatAm to remain relatively modest compared with traditional demand drivers, at least through the end of the decade. Under the MS Bull Case scenario, we estimate that DC capacity would add ~11GW of new electricity demand by 2030 (~7.9 GW in Brazil), equivalent to ~4% of total power demand, from virtually zero today. This would add ~80bp to the overall power demand CAGR in 2025-30. More details in Latam Data Centers - Aiming for a Bull Case (22 Apr 2026). A steepening duck curve and rising curtailment are increasing the need for flexibility. The rapid expansion of intermittent renewable generation across LatAm, particularly in Brazil and Chile, has led to increasingly pronounced duck curves, with growing midday oversupply followed by steeper evening ramps as solar generation declines. At the same time, renewable curtailment has increased significantly, exceeding 20% of potential generation in some recent months in Brazil. These trends highlight the growing mismatch between when electricity is generated and when it is needed, reinforcing the need for flexible resources to shift energy across hours, reduce curtailment and support system reliability.

records.text: Methodological Notes Market pricing: In order to compute the market pricing for central bank meetings, 1. we leverage GS Quant to extract the market implied interest rate from an OIS receiver curve with a 1d maturity contract. We extract the implied interest rate from a contract that matures the Friday before the week ahead, and take the difference with a contract that matures the Friday after the week ahead, attributing the difference in the market implied rate to the central bank decision expected by market participants. If a country does not have an OIS curve, we do not include a measure of market pricing except for Brazil, where we use the pricing from the CDIE Bloomberg page. Out-of-consensus score: The out-of-consensus score is a normalized indicator of 2. how far out-of-consensus our country teams’ forecasts are. We first compute the historical surprise for all the indicators that we forecast. To do so, we take the difference between the Bloomberg consensus and the actual data print for each indicator from the year 2000 onward. We then take the standard deviation of these series for each indicator and use it to normalize the difference between our forecasts and consensus. Effectively, this allows us to see how far out-of-consensus our forecasts are in a harmonized and normalized metric across indicators. Stagflation tends to weigh on equities and bonds together, and has historically coincided with strong gold performance. records.text: II. Coffee Outlook: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly Both arabica and robusta supply is plentiful this year, next year’s harvest is at risk, and exchange stocks are thin enough to keep front-month futures prices volatile. Good: The physical market should loosen in 2026/27. Brazil’s 2026 on-year arabica crop is strong by most estimates (Conab: 48.2mn bags, +35% yoy; USDA: 47.5mn, +25% yoy). Vietnam’s robusta crop should also be strong after ample irrigation water through the early-2026 dry season, before El Niño developed in June (USDA: 31.4mn bags, +3% yoy). The USDA expects global coffee production to exceed consumption by ~10mn bags in 2026/27. Bad: The 2027/28 crop is already at risk. Brazil’s 2027 arabica crop is an off-year and an unusually wet winter (+207%2 vs. normal) could potentially trigger uneven flowering. In Vietnam, the super El Niño has already drawn down groundwater, similar to 2023 (light blue line in Exhibit 6, Right Panel). If groundwater does not recover before the rains end around November, farmers could enter the December-April dry season with insufficient irrigation water, putting the 2027/28 robusta crop in Vietnam at risk (close to a replay of 2024). Ugly: Because only a small share of global coffee is eligible for delivery against ICE futures, low ICE certified stocks could keep the futures curve in backwardation and front-month prices highly volatile even as physical supply improves this year. records.text: M Global Foundation 6 Japan Growth: AI-linked investment supports activity, but household demand remains fragile • Global AI demand continues to support Japanese exports, semiconductor manufacturing equipment, and corporate profits, offsetting some of the deterioration in the terms of trade from higher energy-import costs. Stronger external demand is increasingly supporting domestic investment. • The benefits are extending into data centers, advanced manufacturing and related infrastructure. However, real household income and consumption continue to recover gradually, while higher borrowing costs are beginning to restrain housing and other rate-sensitive activity. • The September Tankan suggests that previous rate increases have not materially tightened corporate financial conditions, leaving room for further normalization. The key question is whether stronger corporate earnings and investment translate into sustained household income and consumption growth. Inflation: Imported costs are rising faster than underlying domestic inflation • We expect Japan-style core CPI, which includes energy, to accelerate toward 3%Y in December, reflecting elevated crude import prices, yen weakness, and higher goods prices. The outlook also depends on the continuation of government energy subsidies in 2027. • Firms' willingness to raise prices and higher inflation expectations have strengthened the BoJ's assessment of underlying inflation risks. While data centers remain the most immediate catalyst, we see industrial reshoring as an increasingly important and potentially underappreciated driver of electricity demand, with growth expected to accelerate more meaningfully post-2030. Supported by bipartisan policy backing and attractive incentives, efforts to rebuild domestic manufacturing capacity could create an additional market for onsite power solutions. In collaboration with our Multi-Industrials team, we have sized the potential electricity demand associated with a resurgence in US manufacturing. Under a scenario in which the US increases its share of global manufacturing output to 20% by 2050 (vs. 16% in 2025), we estimate as much as 113GW of incremental electricity capacity could be required through 2035, including commercial demand, to support this trajectory. Given existing grid constraints, we believe onsite generation could play an increasingly important role in enabling this industrial expansion, extending the growth runway for BTM providers well beyond the initial data center buildout. However, additional nuclear restarts are making Japan’s grid less flexible in accommodating variable generation from renewables. Because these baseload plants cannot ramp down quickly when solar output peaks at midday, the grid struggles to absorb additional renewable generation. This dynamic makes gas-fired power particularly important for maintaining grid stability. The structural bottleneck was evident in March–April 2026, when the Tokyo metropolitan area curtailed up to 4.41GW of local solar generation while simultaneously importing power from the Tohoku region to maintain inflexible thermal and nuclear minimums. Grid operators will continue to keep baseload assets online at minimum capacity. We therefore believe Japan will require greater investment in batteries and new grid connections, while continuing to rely on the LNG supply chain. records.text: Coffee: The Good, the Bad, and the Ugly Coffee prices have already fallen in anticipation of the strong 2026 crop, with arabica (the premium bean) down ~10% YTD and robusta (the cheaper bean used in instant coffee) down ~15% YTD (Exhibit 1). The physical market should loosen as the widely expected strong harvest improves global supply. Because only a small share of global coffee is eligible for delivery against ICE futures, low ICE certified stocks could keep the futures curve in backwardation and front-month prices highly volatile even as physical supply improves this year, while early signs point to renewed supply risks in 2027/28. In this Agriculture Analyst, we first provide a brief primer on how the coffee market works and the indicators that can signal supply almost a year before harvest. We then use that framework to assess the 2026/27 crop and the emerging risks to the 2027/28 crop. I. An Overview of the Coffee Market The world drinks about 175-180 million bags of coffee a year1 (one bag is 60kg of “green” unroasted beans). Around 60% is arabica, the milder, pricier bean behind most café and specialty coffee. The other 40% is robusta, which is cheaper, more bitter and higher in caffeine, and forms the base of instant coffee and most espresso blends. Coffee demand is relatively price-insensitive, reflecting habitual consumption and the small share of beans in the retail price of a cup. The IEA estimates that cooling can account for approximately one-third of India's electricity consumption on hot summer nights, compared with just over 10% on an annual basis, illustrating its disproportionate impact on load profiles. As AC penetration rises, this growing concentration of demand during evening and nighttime hours increases requirements for dependable generation, storage and grid flexibility. We are more constructive than the IEA on the need for dependable power: Our global demand forecast is ~60bps above the IEA through 2030 (Exhibit 17), with the largest divergence in the US and Australia, while China and India are broadly aligned. In our view, the upside risk is greatest in markets where data centers are being layered on top of stronger industrial, commercial and cooling demand, increasing the risk that consumption grows faster than generation and grid capacity can respond.

Not least given that France's fiscal woes have pushed long-end EGB yields higher, which as President Lagarde recently noted, is already doing some of the ECB's tightening work. The real money picture for EGBs is more mixed than a simple “buy the dip” story. Investors still hold substantial two- and five-year exposure relative to history, but recent flows into both are exceptionally weak (Figure 4). Ten-year bonds are the exception: holdings remain low in their historical range, while above-median flows point to renewed buying. That interest has not extended to the long end, where 30-year flows remain subdued despite holdings sitting close to the midpoint. EUR demand is also unconvincing, with both holdings and flows below their historical medians. The takeaway is selective demand rather than a broad return to euro-area assets. Some investors are adding ten-year exposure, but there is little evidence here that higher yields are drawing buyers across the curve or providing fresh support for the EUR. CITI'S TAKE An apparent change of emphasis in ECB communication from the first pillar of its decision framework (inflation outlook) to the other two (underlying inflation dynamics and policy transmission) justifies market expectations of a more moderate path for policy rates. This change also highlights what we see as a relative instability of the ECB reaction function recently. This may change soon. We believe the President of the ECB may announce her early departure soon (Bloomberg, 30-Sep), given that it would facilitate government decisions on the quasi-simultaneous replacement of half of the Executive Board in early 2027. It does matter then to understand how candidates to her succession believe price formation to take place, as this is the key to the reaction function. We take this opportunity to explain what “hawk” and “dove” really mean in the context of monetary policy. Low groundwater limits irrigation, weakening flowering and crop potential before the rains return (Exhibit 5). records.text: M Global Insight 16 Thirty-Six Trillion Units of Consumption: It's Electric We estimate ~36trn units of power will be consumed by 2030, well in excess of IEA forecasts, with consumption of power outside China growing 3.3x faster than during the last decade (Exhibit 16). This is placing increased pressure on the power system – as power prices rise, the need for grid deployment accelerates and costs continue to inflate. In addition, shifting load patterns are making electron delivery to end consumers even more complex. Increasing amounts of nuclear power (inflexible supply) and renewables (variable supply) is adding to power prices and the need for behind-the-meter supply, especially as the cost to source stable power from the grid rises. AI will contribute ~26% of incremental power consumption over 2026-30e, we estimate (Exhibit 18). We think the BoC and BoE will no longer look through the shock, and we expect them to hike at their next meetings – before second-round inflation shows in data. Our recent work (see Food & Energy, When Non-Core Inflation Shocks Begin to Matter) showed that the pass-through of energy and the growth-inflation trade-off increases with a longer shock. Inventories, contracts, hedges, and margins initially absorb higher costs to varying degrees, while rerouting and physical buffers help preserve activity. As the shock moves through a second and third quarter, however, those cushions become less effective. This transition is becoming visible in shipping costs and refined products, two channels that can amplify other upstream pressures. Shipping costs are raising the price of both energy and goods delivered. Transpacific container rates have risen sharply, congestion through Panama has increased, and diversions around the Red Sea have lengthened shipping times. More striking, freight on a benchmark Middle East-to-China route was typically around $1-3/bbl over the past five years but is now well above to $30/bbl. We expect another hike in December . A further rise beyond that cannot be ruled out but is not our base case given the tightening in financial conditions and our expectation of a fall in energy prices into 2027 . Recent bond market volatility has also raised the question of whether the ECB should intervene. We think ECB President Christine Lagarde is likely to stress that it has the tools it needs, and stands ready to act to counter disorderly market dynamics. Relatedly, we believe that the widening of OAT spreads over the past week has been largely driven by sentiment rather than fundamentals, amid limited flows. This dynamic has seen risk premium take prices to oversold levels, in our view. Historical analysis of the credit spline and previous episodes of sovereign stress suggest that risk –reward now favors being long OATs. On a new- issue basis the 5s20s spread has narrowed by 25.5bp from 164.0bp at entry to 138.5bp on Thursday 22 October, a gain of +25.1bp in DV01 terms, or +3.58 yen per 100 yen face of the 20y leg. The worst mark was 5bp against us on the day after entry; the position never came close to the stop. The trade did what it was designed to do. Front-loaded hike pricing pushed the 5y up 34.5bp while the 20y, bid at every auction, rose only 9.0bp, and the bear flattening delivered the 25.5bp. There are three reasons to book the gain now. Recent project approvals and the draft PDP 2026 reinforce the direction of travel, with direct PPAs, data center growth and new power infrastructure becoming increasingly aligned. Malaysia and Singapore remain large markets, but as spare capacity tightens, we expect gas-fired generation, grids and renewable PPAs to become increasingly important enablers of further AI investment. India: India’s installed data center power capacity has risen to around 1.57GW as of August 2026, from ~375MW in 2020, with government estimates pointing to nearly 8GW by 2030. More importantly for power markets, the government’s estimate for incremental AI data center load by F32 has risen sharply to 26.3GW, almost double the 13.6GW estimate published earlier this year. Large hyperscaler commitments, new AI-ready campuses and state-level policies are broadening development beyond the traditional Mumbai hub, making generation and transmission availability increasingly important constraints. records.text: Methodology Notes for GS High Frequency Oil Products Indicators 1. Global refinery runs: We use timely, high-frequency Kpler data on visible refinery runs to forecast global and regional (OECD and non-OECD) refinery runs from the IEA. IEA monthly refinery runs data typically come with a three-month lag, so we use a simple month-over-month regression model to nowcast IEA runs through the latest month of fully realized Kpler data (i.e. the month before the ongoing one). We then convert realized IEA and predicted monthly global runs into a weekly series using weekly variation in Kpler data. We also use weekly changes in Kpler refinery runs to nowcast refinery runs for the current ongoing month, which does not yet have a full month of realized data (latest methodology here). 2. OECD commercial stocks nowcast: Our OECD commercial stocks nowcast estimates OECD commercial inventory levels by integrating monthly inventory statistics published by the International Energy Agency (IEA) with weekly US inventory data from the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) via a regression approach. 3. India oil demand nowcast: Our India oil demand nowcast estimates total Indian oil demand for months not yet realized in International Energy Agency (IEA) demand data via a regression approach that integrates more timely data from India’s Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas covering total monthly oil demand as well as data published biweekly by Bloomberg News covering Indian retail fuel sales. 4.

Exhibit 14 shows historical examples of where gold has rallied during shock events. However, most of these are demand shocks, which often provide a supportive backdrop for gold. Equities sell off, bond yields fall and monetary policy is often eased to combat growth concerns. In this situation, gold benefits as the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset declines. In contrast, supply shocks bring greater inflation risks. The Middle East conflict has created a global energy supply shock. The inflation risk has driven interest hikes with potentially more to come, while long-dated bond yields have also rallied. Gold is a non- yielding asset and so struggles to compete for a place in investor portfolios in this environment. Also see metal&ROCK: Gold: Safe Haven or Risk Asset? (17 Apr 2026).
